Variants.Content: Oldtown in the North is the traditional seat of House Locke and should not be confused with Oldtown in the Reach. The name itself illustrates the simple naming of ancient settlements in the north: the ancient stone walls, repaired towers, farmland and villages that continue around the castle are enough to become the center of a place. The Locke family belongs to the vassal system in the north, inheriting the legacy of the ancestors and their obligations to Winterfell; but their daily life is inseparable from the more common problems in the north - long winter, roads, food, horses, and mutual aid or friction between neighboring lords. The "oldness" of the old city does not mean stagnation, but the layers left behind after many generations of continuous maintenance, guarding, and farming. Who owns it is variable, this hierarchy does not change easily.

Entry Oldcastle Local families also rely on firewood, hunting grounds, peat, salt fish, and granaries to survive the long winter; if any road, well, spring, or wharf fails, the price will fall on them first.

Entry Oldcastle They also recognize the accents, laws, and credentials of the North; reputations can travel great distances from taverns, but true distances must still be measured by wheel, oar, or horse's hoof.

Entry Oldcastle If you can supply supplies, avoid danger, and find a guide, it is worth marking in your itinerary; if you don't have these three things, no matter how loud your family name is, it won't be able to save the lost.

From workshops to sanctuaries, the Old City juxtaposes stone walls, wooden beams, iron doors, tombs and seams repaired by generations with old gods, weirwoods and ancestral graveyards. A stronghold was therefore not just a lord's hall, but also a place where weddings and funerals, vows, labor and local memories recurred.

Entry Oldcastle They care about firewood, hunting grounds, peat, salt fish, and granaries that can survive the long winter. They also care about whether seeds are left after the grain collection and whether the city gates are open in times of disaster. When people from afar see coats of arms, they see whether there will be food to eat tomorrow.
